item.title: How Do You Run for Office in a Gang War?
item.description:
Gang violence in Haiti is so bad that Antoine Rodon Bien-Aimé, a candidate for the Haitian Senate, has been campaigning via speakerphone and video calls to community meetings.

Elections — the first in a decade — are scheduled for Dec. 13, but kidnappings and killings are pervasive. Mr. Bien-Aimé, a former deputy in the legislature, rattled off the names of various neighborhoods around the capital where he cannot meet voters.

“We can’t go and campaign on the field,” he said. “We are scared. I am scared to drive. I am scared to go out of the house, because I’m scared to be kidnapped.”

Mr. Bien-Aimé is one of a growing chorus of voices who believe the Haitian government, under pressure from the United States, has rushed to hold elections at any cost. Critics argue that too many swaths of the Haitian electorate have been forced from their homes and would be unable to cast ballots.

With major highways in the control of armed groups, it will be difficult to move not just candidates, but also ballots. Entire communities risk being cut off from the vote.

Many people believe the election date is essentially fiction — a goal that even Haitian officials do not believe possible.

But as Haiti enters its second decade without elections to fill a single government office, the push for a return to democracy is real.

While many people argue that you can’t hold elections without security, government officials and some experts strongly argue the opposite: that Haiti will never be safe if it doesn’t start electing its own leaders.

Still, many Haitians face a reality that is all too dangerous, as a massacre in a well-heeled community in the outskirts of the capital last week reminded many.

“We want to go to elections,” Mr. Bien-Aimé said. “But we want to go to well-prepared, good elections.”

Haiti last held elections in November 2016, when Jovenel Moïse, a banana exporter, was elected amid delays and accusations of widespread fraud. He was assassinated in July 2021, and then the gang violence that had always been common in Haiti quickly spread. In early 2024, it exploded into a kind of war.

Armed groups that had fought each other for years, sometimes doing the bidding of corrupt politicians, joined forces. They attacked police stations, prisons, hospitals and neighborhoods. The prime minister was forced out and the airport was closed for months.

More than 1.5 million Haitian people have fled their homes, and nearly 250,000 of them are living in squalor in impromptu displacement sites, such as public schools.

The United Nations said 3,050 people, including those targeted by law enforcement, were killed in the first half of this year.

Gangs control some 70 percent of Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, and have spread to other regions outside the city, including the rural Artibonite Valley.

With the security situation so volatile, elections were postponed several times. The race to elect the legislature is now six years overdue.

Although the government insists that it is moving forward with Dec. 13 election, most experts believe that date borders on fantasy.

The United States has spent hundreds of millions of dollars on security efforts in Haiti, and experts say Washington has been a big factor in pressing Haitian officials to move forward. After months of delays, the Haitian government formed an electoral council, published the required election decree and came up with the December date.

“It won’t be a Cadillac election,” Michael Kozak, a former senior U.S. State Department official, told a House committee last month, while he was still in his post. “But if it’s a good, you know, F-150 election, that’s going to be solid. They need an elected government. It doesn’t need to be perfect.”

But many critics say it’s preposterous to hold an election that disenfranchises the cities where most voters live. Only candidates who can afford helicopters would be able to fly over gang checkpoints on major highways to canvas regions outside the capital. Millions of people have to register to vote, a process the government is unlikely to be able to pull off in time.

Lemoine Bonneau, a former newspaper columnist who is now a politician, said the government seems poised to simply abandon dozens of decisive neighborhoods where it will be impossible to set up polling stations.

“So, electors are going to vote in Upper Artibonite Valley, and in Lower Artibonite they won’t go to the polls?” he said. “In the 10 communities in the West Department, there will be no elections, and there will be no lawmakers there?”

Senators who secure just 15 percent of the vote could wind up winning a race to represent the West Department, where Port-au-Prince is, because only the people in safe areas voted, a possibility Mr. Bonneau called “scandalous.”

Patrice Dumont, a former senator who has not yet registered to run in the elections, said a history of substandard elections is a reason Haiti has gotten so bad, and they can’t be done halfway.

Some critics accuse the prime minister, Alix Didier Fils-Aimé, of secretly wanting to stall elections because that would allow him to stay in power longer.

Mr. Fils-Aimé did not respond to requests for comment. He has publicly said that people are clamoring for elections, and that insecurity should not be a reason to boycott the race.

Jerry Tardieu, a former congressman who hopes to run for president, agreed.

“This prolonged transition is taking its toll on the Haitian people,” he said. “The truth is that, for a long time, Haiti will not have the ideal conditions for peaceful elections like we have had in the past. If we wait for these conditions, there will not be elections in Haiti for a very long time.”

Jacques Desrosiers, the president of Haiti’s Provisional Electoral Council, said in an interview that he “remains convinced” that Dec. 13 is a doable date, but he acknowledged that the country needs better security.

Mr. Derosiers said liberating the main roads from gang control would be key, because it would significantly reduce the government’s logistics costs.

“We also need state presence restored in certain communes to facilitate electoral operations, even at a minimum level,” he said. “We have the commitment of law enforcement and government authorities, who have pledged to work toward creating this acceptable climate.”

He stressed that the electoral council was counting on help from law enforcement and international partners to help make that happen.

This year, a multinational, U.N.-backed mission meant to go after the gangs, called the Gang Suppression Force, arrived in Haiti.

Although the gang suppression force has people from Chad, El Salvador, Guatemala, Jamaica, Mongolia, and Sri Lanka, experts say it currently has only about 20 percent of its intended 5,500 members.

The Haitian government has also contracted with the American private military contractor Erik Prince to help conduct drone strikes in gang-controlled neighborhoods.

The drone task force has yet to announce the capture or killing any major gang leader.

A person close to the task force operations who was not authorized to speak publicly, said the group has helped reduce the gang foothold in the capital from 90 percent of the city early last year to 70 percent now.

The government plans to take more territory with the help of the gang-suppression force and increased police recruits. The team was recently able to enter Village de Dieu, the stronghold of a gang leader known as Izo, for the first time in five years. Earlier this year in January, it wounded Jimmy “Barbecue” Chérizier, a notorious gang leader whose home and base was destroyed.

Alexandre Carrie, 34, who recently registered to vote at a school in Pétion-Ville, a suburb outside the capital, agreed that the election must go on. But the government must find a way for the people in gang-controlled areas like Croix des Bouquets and Cité Soleil to participate, he said.

“There are honest people who live there; it’s not just criminals,” he said. “As soon as the government provides security and the criminals give the people a chance to hold the elections, I think everything will be fine.”

He added, “The country has reached its limit; we can’t continue to sink."

item.title: Norway Seizes Russian Ship, Testing Moscow in the High Arctic
item.description:
For the past several days, Norwegian security services had been tracking a Russian research ship.

It was cruising around Svalbard, an icy archipelago high in the Arctic near the North Pole that Norway controls but is governed by a one-of-a-kind treaty that gives the Russians access.

On Wednesday, the Norwegians pounced.

Armed with a court order that is part of a global effort to recover Russian assets, Norwegian police officers boarded the ship while it was docked in Barentsburg, a tiny Russian outpost in Svalbard. The officers confronted the captain of the ship, a somewhat clunky, 200-foot-long oceanographic vessel, and announced that they were “arresting” it.

The seized ship was part of a broader effort to enforce an international court judgment ordering Russia to pay a Ukrainian energy company, Naftogaz, more than $4 billion for expropriating that company’s assets in Crimea. The ship, owned by the Russian government and called Professor Molchanov, after a famous Russian scientist, is now prohibited from leaving Barentsburg until Norwegian courts decide what to do next.

“We have only acted as a messenger,” said Lars Fause, the governor of Svalbard.

He added that it was the first time Norway had taken action like this in Svalbard. The Russians quickly denounced it, with the foreign ministry spokeswoman calling it “piracy.” But the bold move fits neatly with the shifting geopolitics in this part of the Arctic and Norway’s increasingly aggressive stance.

For years, Svalbard was a collegial place, remote and often bone-chillingly cold. But it was one where Russians, Norwegians and people from all over the world went snowmobiling together, scouted polar bears and slurped borscht at chess tournaments. Svalbard’s remoteness and extreme northern latitude — it stretches as far as 81 degrees north — make it an ideal place to study climate change and Earth’s atmosphere.

The cluster of islands is part of Norway but governed by a unique treaty, dating from the aftermath of World War I, that allows just about anyone to take up a life there, visa free. The Russians used this treaty to set up a few coal-mining towns decades ago, including Barentsburg, and a few hundred Russians still live there and dig coal. For years, the Norwegians basically left them alone.

But as the Arctic region has become more strategically contested, and after Western European countries lined up against Russia in the wake of Moscow’s war in Ukraine, Svalbard, in turn, has become a reflection of a new, sharper-elbowed world.

The Norwegians are defending this part of the Arctic as never before, increasing surveillance, taking rights away from foreigners and putting more restrictions on international scientists. They are especially wary of Russian vessels prowling around Svalbard’s seas.

Russian state media said the research ship had been taking about 20 artists to Barentsburg for a special exhibition. Yuri Trutnev, a Russian presidential envoy, called the seizure “a really strange thing to do.”

“We have a treaty on Svalbard. It’s been around for decades,” he said. That treaty has now been violated, he added.

Norway’s ambassador to Moscow met with officials at the Russian foreign ministry, and the Norwegian authorities said they would help “take care of the crew and passengers” who were on Professor Molchanov when it was seized.

But several academics who study this part of the world said the ship was a well-known propaganda tool and that for years it had been ferrying Russian agents to Svalbard who then raised Russian flags and boosted Russian claims to the archipelago, in addition to performing surveillance.

“The ship has been used for Russian hybrid operations,” said Kari Aga Myklebost, a professor of Russian history at the Arctic University of Norway in Tromso.

She said that Norway should “put its foot down” and that the country “needs to send a clear message to Russia that Norway does not accept hybrid operations in Norwegian waters or in Svalbard.”

Norway has been closely monitoring all types of Russian vessels in recent years. Norwegian intelligence officials have said that the Kremlin frequently uses civilian personnel and nonmilitary vessels with legitimate access to Norwegian ports to gather intelligence. Russian spies are especially interested in Norway’s defense technology and weapons capabilities, Norwegian reports said.

Norway is now testing whether its courts have authority over Russian property in a region with a longstanding Russian presence, said Anthony Heron, a researcher at the Arctic Institute, an international research center headquartered in Washington.

Like the governments of Britain, France and other European nations, the Norwegians are stepping up legal action where Russian assets are exposed and reachable, he added.

“Although it’s just a legal enforcement action, not a security incident, it lands in an especially sensitive spot geographically,” Mr. Heron said.He said the seizure of this ship in Svalbard could push the limits of how far Norwegian sovereignty “extends in Moscow’s eyes.”

Alina Lobzina contributed reporting.

item.title: Workers Rescued From Tunnel in Nepal 9 Days After Flood
item.description:
At least two workers trapped in one of the hydropower project tunnels hit by Nepal’s flash flood last week were rescued on Friday morning, an army spokesman said.

Officers from the Nepali Army, with assistance from technical teams sent by India, China and other countries, have been working day and night to make their way through a dense mixture of sludge and mud to bore into the tunnels.

Hundreds of workers have been missing in the tunnels since last Wednesday, when a glacial collapse sent tsunami-like waves of water mixed with rock and debris through two river valleys, killing more than 1,200 people. More than 4,000 people remain missing in Nepal and neighboring Tibet.

Raja Ram Basnet, a spokesman for the Nepali Army, said the workers were rescued from the Trishuli 3A hydropower project.

The Nepali government reported a week ago that more than 900 people were missing in the tunnels, after hydroelectric producers submitted their tally of workers unaccounted for. For days there had been dwindling hope of finding survivors.

To try and get to missing workers, rescue teams have had to dig through dense mud and debris, then bore through thick tunnel doors or walls, or blast them open with explosives. Some of the tunnels were filled with the sludge swept in by the flood

On Saturday, the army said that two thermal drones used by the Nepal Army had not detected any signs of life, but that the search would continue. Late that night, Sudan Gurung, the home minister of Nepal, said on social media that rescuers had reached the crown of the Trishuli 3A tunnel and had started supplying air through the hole while they conducted excavation work.

Nepal has built a robust hydroelectric industry, harnessing the fast-flowing waters in the Himalayas to generate megawatts of electricity. Those projects, which require both manual and engineering work to construct deep tunnel systems, have also attracted foreign investments. Many hydropower projects were built along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli Rivers, which bore the brunt of the flooding.

item.title: Haze From Indonesian Wildfires Blankets Parts of Malaysia and Philippines
item.description:
Toxic haze and smoke from wildfires in Indonesia that have been intensifying for weeks has spread hundreds of miles across seas, shrouding a vast swath of Southeast Asia in bad air and raising fears of a regional health crisis.

On Friday, Malaysia, among the worst affected of Indonesia’s neighbors, declared a state of emergency in a town in the state of Sarawak, which abuts some of the most fire-stricken Indonesian provinces on the island of Borneo. Sarawak last month temporarily shut down hundreds of schools because of poor air quality.

Across the South China Sea, Kuala Lumpur, the country’s capital on Peninsular Malaysia, has been engulfed by smoke from fires burning on the Indonesian island of Sumatra, to the south. Some parents are keeping their children home from school, said Geraldine Arulsamy, the head of a local Montessori school.

“We can actually smell the poor air quality,” said Ms. Arulsamy, who added that some children had fallen ill.

Irfan Zulkarnain, a fruit stall worker in the city, said a nosebleed and coughing fit had recently sent him to a doctor, who told him his symptoms were from the haze and prescribed him medication.

“But I still have work here at the stall, outside in the heat,” he said.

In neighboring Singapore, where some areas of the city have become clouded by sepia-toned smog, the authorities have urged the public to be on alert for worsening air quality in the next two weeks. More than 1,000 miles east, in Cebu, a city in the central Philippines, Edrine Durante, a 27-year-old resident, said the air felt thick and greasy from the smoke.

“It would normally look bluish, but now it is gray,” she said of the view from her window.

It is a sign of how dire this year’s fires are.

“For a long time, the Philippines was largely insulated from this,” said Gerry Bagtasa, an atmospheric physicist at the University of the Philippines, referring to the trans-boundary smoke. But this year, even Manila, the capital, which lies 350 miles north of Cebu, had received a share of it, he added.

Indonesia, a vast archipelago that stretches across three time zones, is currently in the midst of what some experts fear is shaping up to be the worst fire season in years. More than 490,000 acres of land have burned since the beginning of this year, according to the country’s forest ministry. In addition to the impact on human health, the fires and choking smoke are imperiling the country’s wildlife, including threatened species. In Borneo, at least one orangutan has died from inhaling the smoke, the ministry said.

Driving the fires, in part, is a powerful El Niño, a weather phenomenon marked by shifting ocean temperatures that brings drought to countries such as Indonesia, while unleashing torrents of rain on others.

In the first 10 days of August, more than 90 percent of Indonesia had little to no rainfall, according to the country’s meteorological agency. That month, the number of fire hot spots in peatlands — a type of fire-prone landscape — soared to more than 160,000 from around 45,000, according to data from Pantau Gambut, a nonprofit organization that tracks forest fires in Indonesia.

That surpassed the number of peatland hot spots recorded over the same period in 2015, according to Wahyu Perdana, a spokesman for the group. That was another fire season made devastating by El Niño, when the government said about 6.4 million acres burned.

While El Niño has historically exacerbated fires, experts have long pointed to the degradation of Indonesia’s peatlands as the deeper reason that fires in recent years have so easily spiraled out of control.

A type of spongy wetland, peatlands are resistant to fire in their natural, waterlogged state. But much of the country’s stock has been dried by decades of large-scale plantation farming of cash crops like palm oil, leaving behind a highly potent fuel. Forestry experts and government officials have said that human activity, such as companies or individuals deliberately burning them to clear land, is also largely to blame for peatlands catching fire in the first place.

“Once drained peat ignites, combustion continues underground for weeks, generating dense trans-boundary haze,” Mr. Wahyu said, adding that around a fourth of the peatland fire hot spots recorded in August were located in plantation concessions.

Emilia, a 40-year-old smallholder rubber farmer on Sumatra who like many Indonesians goes by one name, said that fires routinely break out around this time of year as the 49,000-acre sugar cane plantation just across from her village begins its harvest. This season has been no different.

Sometimes the smoke is so thick that visibility shrinks to about 10 feet, she said, adding that it enters kitchens and bedrooms, triggering respiratory illnesses. On Thursday, the fire spread to her own farm, filling her with financial despair. Still, none of the 1,300 villagers have evacuated.

“Where else would we go?” she said.

item.title: U.N. Approves African Proposal for a New World Map
item.description:
The United Nations General Assembly on Friday endorsed a world map that depicts the size of Africa more accurately than the map most commonly used now.

The assembly approved a resolution favoring the Equal Earth projection, a map that supporters say shows the true size of countries, over the familiar Mercator map, which shrinks regions near the Equator. It passed with 164 votes in favor and six abstentions, according to Reuters. The only nation that voted against the resolution was the United States, which said the map promoted an “ideological agenda” and was a distraction from the “genuine problems of international peace, prosperity or good relations,” Reuters reported.

The new map has supporters in Africa, who say the Mercator projection has contributed to a historical bias that has minimized tropical and equatorial regions and exaggerated the size of countries near the poles.

The U.N. resolution does not outlaw the Mercator projection or require the use of the Equal Earth map. But it is part of a campaign to raise awareness of the effects of visual representations of the Earth on how people view the world.

Here’s what to know about the debate.

The projection, one of many ways to represent the spherical Earth on a flat plane, was designed by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate.

It was created by projecting the Earth’s features onto a cylinder, then flattening that into a rectangle.

The map was invaluable for seafaring: Any straight line drawn on the map represents a compass direction that sailors can use to determine which way to go. The projection has since become widely used in books, classrooms and online services like Google Maps.

Every map projection makes sacrifices, like shape, size or distance: You can’t flatten a round object without somehow stretching, shrinking or tearing it. The Mercator projection reflects true directions but distorts the size of landmasses.

If you had a Mercator projection on your classroom wall, you might have grown up believing that Greenland, for example, is as big as Africa, even though it is one-14th its size. You might also think that Alaska is bigger than Mexico, when it is 25 percent smaller.

Critics have argued that the Mercator map creates a subtle bias whereby northern nations, including some of the world’s wealthiest, appear large and equatorial regions, home mostly to developing countries, are depicted as small. Some cartographers say it reinforces a Eurocentric and colonial worldview.

The Equal Earth projection — created in 2018 by the cartographers Bojan Savric, Bernhard Jenny and Tom Patterson — sacrifices straight-line directions in order to render landmasses in their correct proportions. It has rounded edges to account for the Earth’s spherical shape instead of a rectangle.

Advocacy groups in Africa have campaigned to replace the Mercator map since April 2025. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August that year, urging its 55 member states to adopt the Equal Earth map in schools and public communications. The West African nation of Togo sponsored the U.N. resolution, backed by other countries in the African Union.

“A map is never neutral,” Robert Dussey, the foreign minister of Togo, said on Thursday, promoting the U.N. resolution. “It shapes perceptions, influences how the place of peoples and continents in the world is understood and may, sometimes from the earliest years of schooling, perpetuate representations that do not correspond to geographic reality.”

The resolution before the U.N. General Assembly calls on the more than 190 member states to update their educational materials and educate students about the accurate sizes of countries and the limitations of different map projections.

It also urges major digital map providers to discuss the issue with governments and adopt more accurate cartographic representations.

The resolution is not binding. But the push to replace the Mercator map has made progress in other ways.

Google, which used a Mercator-based map for more than a decade, shifted in 2018 to showing the Earth as a globe when zoomed out on the desktop platform. “Greenland’s projection is no longer the size of Africa,” the company said on social media.

Some schools have begun replacing Mercator maps. Boston Public Schools in 2017 began purchasing maps with the Peters projection, which shows countries in their correct proportional sizes to one another at the cost of stretching and squashing their outlines.

The shift was part of the district’s effort to “decolonize the curriculum,” Colin Rose, then a district administrator, told The Boston Globe.

item.title: Timothy Carney, Diplomat Who Went Places Others Avoided, Dies at 82
item.description:
Timothy Carney, a diplomat who relished difficult assignments in war-torn countries and pushed against bureaucratic restrictions, died on Aug. 10 at his home in Cambridge, Mass. He was 82.

His death, from cancer, was confirmed by his wife, Victoria Butler.

In a State Department career that took him from Saigon and Phnom Penh during the Vietnam War, to South Africa during the final years of apartheid, to ambassadorships in Sudan and Haiti as those countries disintegrated, to Iraq after the U.S. invasion, Mr. Carney proved willing to challenge conventional thinking and to go places other diplomats avoided.

He foresaw the looming menace of the Khmer Rouge dictatorship in Cambodia in the mid-1970s, and engaged with Afrikaners in the mid-1980s, convinced they were opening up to the idea of majority rule in South Africa. He opposed closing the U.S. embassy in Khartoum, the capital of Sudan, in 1996 while Osama Bin Laden established himself there — the closure deprived America of a valuable listening post. He was skeptical of the former Haiti president Jean-Bertrand Aristide, seen by many in Washington as a valuable ally, as Mr. Aristide prepared to retake power. In Iraq, Mr. Carney was publicly disgusted with the absence of American planning.

Colleagues said he didn’t hesitate to engage with U.S. foes, believing that to be the diplomats’ best role. “He wasn’t afraid of anybody,” the former U.S. ambassador Robin Raphel, who knew Mr. Carney for decades, said in an interview.

“You don’t make deals with your friends, you make deals with your enemies,” Ms. Raphel said, describing Mr. Carney as “pro-engagement in a way that makes perfect sense.” She added: “Serious people paid attention to him.”

Unusually for a diplomat, Mr. Carney insisted on seeing things for himself, even at the cost of incurring the wrath of his superiors.

As Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia, was being rocketed by rebels in 1972, Mr. Carney — then a junior official in the U.S. embassy — jumped into a car with a Cambodian journalist and soon found “a little kid” who “had been chopped up by a chunk of casing from this 122 mm rocket, and was dead,” Mr. Carney told an interviewer in 2002 for a State Department oral history project.

Undeterred, “we heard a lot of automatic weapons fire from further south,” he said, “and we drove down there to see what was going on.”

The next day, he reported all of it to his bosses at the embassy. They were horrified.

“One didn’t do that,” Mr. Carney told the interviewer in 2002. “You weren’t supposed to put yourself at risk, which struck me as a very bizarre way to do foreign affairs reporting in a war. You have to get out, meet people, and be out of the embassy as much as you possibly could.”

That approach — leaving the embassy — was, and remains, untypical for State Department officials. In an era of heightened security concerns, American diplomats typically stay behind the embassy’s Marine-guarded walls, venturing out only for official events

“He was where no other foreign service officer would be,” Elizabeth Becker, a journalist with extensive reporting experience in Cambodia, said in an interview. “He treated Cambodians with a kind of dignity I did not see from others.”

In April 1975, with the murderous Khmer Rouge closing in, he drove to the prime minister’s house to urge government ministers to evacuate via helicopter. “Nope,” he recalled. “Only one went with us.”

He followed the same path 10 years later in South Africa, where as a political counselor at the U.S. embassy in Pretoria, he went to parties with Afrikaners, some of whom defended apartheid, while meeting others who were “serious, engaging, ruthless, but they had the real interest” in ending it, unlike more outwardly liberal South Africans who he believed paid lip service to change.

“No matter how unstable the political environment and how tense relations could be, Tim always maintained the highest level of professionalism and tenacity,” former President Bill Clinton, who appointed Mr. Carney as ambassador in Sudan and Haiti, wrote on Facebook after his death. Mr. Clinton added that Mr. Carney “always believed that diplomacy was the essential key to reducing instability and promoting peace and prosperity.”

When Mr. Clinton sent Mr. Carney to Sudan in 1995, the country was a safe harbor for Islamist terrorists, and boiling with insurgency. Bin Laden had found refuge there after leaving Saudi Arabia in 1991. For Mr. Carney it was an ideal spot from which to gauge the terrorist threat ahead.

But officials in Washington, led by Susan Rice, the National Security Council senior director for African Affairs at the time, were nervous about threats to the diplomats in Khartoum, and moved them to Nairobi early in 1996.

For Mr. Carney, it was a big mistake. He had been keeping an eye on Mr. Bin Laden but could no longer do so. “We took our eye off the ball,” he later told Roger Cohen of The New York Times. “We did not know what was happening in Khartoum, a center of extremist Islam.”

The same bluntness characterized his response to the chaos of Haiti, where he arrived as ambassador in January 1998 — “no trees except at the embassy residence” he said in the State Department oral history interview — and quickly took the measure of Mr. Aristide, who was regarded with indulgence on Capitol Hill.

“He was more of the same,” Mr. Carney told the state department interviewer. “He himself certainly tolerates corruption as a way of manipulating people. Interesting.”

Timothy Michael Carney was born on July 12, 1944, in St. Joseph, Mo., one of three children of Col. Clement Carney, a career army officer who was a judge in the Judge Advocate General Corps, and Jane (Byrne) Carney, an English teacher. The family moved often when Mr. Carney was growing up, and two of those years were spent in Taipei.

He graduated from Christian Brothers High School in St. Joseph in 1962, and from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology with a Bachelor of Science in 1966.

His first foreign service job came the following year with a junior posting at the embassy in Vietnam, and from 1969 to 1971 he was posted to the embassy in Lesotho.

After his tour in Cambodia ended in 1975, Mr. Carney studied at Cornell University, served in Washington on the State Department’s Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia desk, and was appointed to the U.S. mission in Thailand from 1979 to 1983.

During the 1990s, Mr. Carney undertook several missions for the United Nations, including as adviser to the U.N. representative in Somalia in 1993.

Mr. Carney retired from the State Department in December 1999. He returned to government service for several months in 2003 as a member of the Office of Reconstruction and Humanitarian Assistance, the agency established under the Department of Defense to help reconstruct Iraq.

He left Baghdad after two months, frustrated by what the writer David Rieff called a “dialogue of the deaf between ORHA officials and the U.S. military on the ground in Iraq.” He returned to Iraq for several months in 2007, and assisted the State Department in Kabul in 2009.

In addition to his wife, a journalist and writer, whom he married in 1983, Mr. Carney is survived by his sister, Sheri Carney; his daughter, Anne Carney, from his previous marriage with Demaz Tep Baker; and two grandchildren.

“Tim was very deeply committed everywhere he served,” Ms. Butler said in an interview. “Everywhere we went he got to know the people where we lived. He believed very strongly in soft power versus hard power. He was an old school kind of diplomat.”

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: 9 Days After Flood, 2 Men Are Pulled Alive From Mud-Filled Tunnels in Nepal
item.description:
The rescuers heard voices. They crawled through a sludge-filled tunnel deep underground where employees of a hydroelectric plant in Nepal had been trapped for nine days.

“We are coming!” Lt. Col. Ganga Baral, one of the leaders of the operation, said he had called out. “Don’t worry, the Nepali Army is coming.”

On Friday morning, two mud-caked survivors were rescued from the tunnels and hoisted into the open air, an extraordinary moment captured on video and in photos by the army.

The improbable rescue provided a measure of hope a week and a half after a glacial collapse unleashed a tsunami of mud and boulders that killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal and Tibet and left thousands of others missing.

The men were rescued from a hydroelectric center buried so deeply in the detritus of the flood that engineers had to use satellite images to pinpoint its location amid the disfigured landscape.

Hirashova Maharjan, the wife of Kabir Maharjan, one of the workers rescued, described her husband as deeply disoriented after being airlifted to Kathmandu, the capital, for medical treatment.

“He didn’t even recognize me,” she said from the army hospital in Kathmandu. But his condition has since improved, she said.

“He is stable now,” she said. “We’re so happy. We are crying with happiness. Thank you to the army and to the government.”

The raging floodwaters that erupted on Aug. 26 washed away roads, bridges and, in some cases, entire villages.

The two men were rescued from a tunnel in the Upper Trishuli 3A hydropower project. The body of a third man, a mechanical engineer, was also recovered on Friday, according to Dirghayu Kumar Shrestha, the head of the Nepal Electricity Authority.

More than 40 other workers were thought to be inside the tunnel, according to Sanjay Sah, one of the rescued men. It was not clear how many were still alive.

Mr. Sah was able to answer questions through an oxygen mask. He spoke from a stretcher in a video that was posted to a government ministry’s Facebook page. He said he thought three or four people were still alive in the area where he had been found.

“I used to work in the control room as an operator,” he says in the video. “Usually there would be four or five people there, but at the time, there were 40 or 45.”

He added: “I tried to get everyone out and tried to warn everyone. But then I ran out of time.”

Mr. Sah, who was a mechanical foreman at the hydroelectric plant, said he had recited prayers “over and over again” during his time trapped underground in darkness. “How many days has it been?” he asked.

The rescue efforts have been grueling. Images posted by the Nepali Army showed rescuers slithering through sludge deep in the tunnels with hard hats and flashlights. Other rescuers paddled through tunnels in inflatable dinghies, the kind used in white-water rafting.

Arnold Dix, an Australian geologist and engineer who is assisting the Nepalese authorities in the rescue operations, said it had taken a day or two to locate the power stations and to develop a plan to rescue the workers.

Nepal has a large hydroelectric industry that harnesses the fast-flowing waters in the Himalayas. Many of the projects have tunnel systems deep in the earth along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, which bore the brunt of the flooding.

Mr. Dix said he had focused on the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, relying on engineering drawings of the structures underground, satellite imagery and old charts to try and identify any potential “Goldilocks zones” — a term he used to describe a small subterranean area “where a human being could have survived.”

Most of the rescue efforts have been focused in the project’s cable tunnel, which runs from the underground powerhouse to the transmission grid.

The operation has been slow and difficult work, Mr. Dix said. Rescuers have had to dig through mud and use explosives to blast through rocks “the size of cars.” Once inside the tunnel, they were faced with water that had to be drained, he added.

Workers had to dig a huge drainage canal back to the river.

“We were worried that the tunnel was full of water, and it would drown us, or maybe drown people who were ahead of us in the tunnel,” Mr. Dix said.

Rescuers were then able to create a small gap along the top of the cable tunnel through which they could crawl, calling to any survivors. That was the area where rescuers found Mr. Maharjan and Mr. Sah.

Mr. Sah’s family had all but given up hope that he might be found alive. Dev Sah, his brother- in-law, said that the family had decided just a day earlier to provide a DNA sample in case his body needed to be identified.

On Friday, Dev Sah said he had spoken to the rescued man at the hospital and had to reassure him repeatedly that he was now safe.

“He has received a new life today,” Dev Sah said.

Mujib Mashal, Alex Travelli and Binod Ghimire contributed reporting.

item.title: Netanyahu Posts A.I. Video Pairing Mamdani With Iranian Ruler
item.description:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel posted an A.I.-produced campaign video on Friday that imagines Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, making common cause with Iran’s supreme leader and others over Israel’s upcoming election.

“Erdogan, bro, are you coming to the party of the fall of Netanyahu’s elections?” a computer-animated version of Mr. Mamdani asks in a phone call with an avatar of Turkey’s president, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, in the video, posted to Mr. Netanyahu’s personal X profile. The images are labeled as A.I.-generated.

The video then shows avatars of Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, the Iranian leader, and Mahmoud Abbas, president of the Palestinian Authority, joining the fictional conversation rejoicing at the prospect that voters will topple Mr. Netanyahu.

Mr. Mamdani’s office declined to comment on the video.

The enmity between the first Muslim mayor of America’s largest city and the longest-serving prime minister of Israel has only intensified in recent weeks. The video offered the latest example of how each leader has made opposition to the other part of their political profile, despite their very different jobs and the thousands of miles between them.

Mr. Netanyahu, who is facing a tough re-election in October and is trailing in the Israeli opinion polls, has accused Mr. Mamdani of “fomenting hate,” and appealed to Israeli national security in criticizing the mayor, partly by including him among Israel’s enemies.

Likud party billboards have plastered Mr. Mamdani’s face alongside the leaders of Iran and Hezbollah, the militant group in Lebanon that Israel has been fighting for decades. The video Mr. Netanyahu posted on Friday ends with him as the election victor, and Israel’s foes calling off the party.

“They want Netanyahu to fall. Don’t let them win,” a narrator says in Hebrew.

Mr. Mamdani, a vocal critic of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, told The New York Times in July that he was looking into whether he could arrest Mr. Netanyahu when he visits the United Nations in September, and he has called the Israeli leader a “war criminal.”

The mayor later acknowledged that he did not have the authority to make good on an arrest, a campaign pledge, but he has urged the federal government to do so.

The International Criminal Court in 2024 issued an arrest warrant for him on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, where more than 70,000 people have been killed in a war sparked by the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023 terrorist attack on Israel. The warrant also sought the arrest of three Hamas leaders, who have all been killed, and a former Israeli defense minister.

But there appears to be no chance of federal law enforcement arresting Mr. Netanyahu, who denies those charges, in the near future. The United States has never joined the court or recognized its authority.

President Trump has said that the Israeli leader, whose country is a longtime American ally, would not be arrested in the United States “in any way, shape, or form.”

Mr. Netanyahu said he still planned to travel to New York City in September for the United Nations General Assembly meeting. Last year, representatives from dozens of countries walked out of the General Assembly just before Mr. Netanyahu gave a defiant speech rejecting the creation of a Palestinian state.

Jonathan Rosen contributed reporting.

item.title: Farage Aides Shown on Video Discussing Secret Donations
item.description:
Two top aides to Nigel Farage, the pugilistic leader of Britain’s right-wing party, were secretly captured on film arranging what they appeared to think were political donations from an American businessman and his British son — a move Mr. Farage on Friday denounced as an “exercise in entrapment” by his enemies.

The aides, Dan Jukes and James Orr, are shown discussing over drinks how the contributions could be secretly funneled to benefit the party, Reform U.K., without disclosure, according to a report on the British TV network Channel 4. Another recording shows Mr. Farage thanking both the father and the son for their support.

In fact, Mr. Farage and his aides were speaking with a journalist and an actor who were posing as the donors, according to Channel 4, which published the report on the eve of Reform’s annual party conference in Birmingham, England.

“The establishment will do everything it can to stop us,” Mr. Farage, visibly angry, said during a news conference there with Jordan Bardella, the president of France’s right-wing National Rally party.

Mr. Farage insisted that Reform had “done nothing wrong, taken no illegal money,” even as the party announced that Mr. Jukes, who has worked with Mr. Farage for years, and Mr. Orr had both stepped down during an internal investigation.

British law requires all donations to be disclosed and prohibits political contributions from foreign sources. But Mr. Farage told reporters on Friday that Mr. Jukes and Mr. Orr had been taken in by “far-left activists.” He said they were guilty of nothing more than “loose pub talk, including a couple of boasts that simply were not true.”

The broadcast of the video was a stunning political blow for a party that has been seeking to turn significant public support into a governing coalition. It forced Mr. Farage and other party leaders to respond to a barrage of news reports even as they tried to remain on message for an estimated 8,000 delegates who streamed into the cavernous conference center.

Keynote speakers pledged action on migration, lower taxes and less regulation for an audience that seemed rattled by what they had hoped would be a celebration of the party’s recent success in local and regional elections. Even the marquee speakers felt compelled to address Thursday’s news.

“We know the establishment will throw every lie, smear and desperate trick at us,” said Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesman, as he vowed that Reform would close down Britain’s borders to illegal immigrants. “But we will prevail.”

Activists from a group called Climate Resistance briefly disrupted the conference on Friday by unrolling a banner that said “Resist Reform” near the entrance of the hall. Several activists also interrupted Mr. Farage’s keynote speech.

Channel 4 said that the discussions about donations involving Mr. Farage and his aides were filmed as part of an elaborate undercover operation conducted by Verbatim Investigations, a group founded by journalists from the Center for Climate Reporting, a nonprofit. The New York Times has not independently verified the actions in the videos.

Before the Channel 4 report on Thursday evening, Mr. Orr had spent the day on several high-profile panels during the start of the party conference. On Friday, Reform announced that the party had opened an internal investigation.

Mr. Orr posted a defense of his actions on social media, saying, “There’s absolutely no way that this could amount to a benefit or a donation in kind at all.” A spokesman for Reform did not immediately respond to a request for comment about Mr. Orr’s and Mr. Jukes’s actions on the video.

The news comes as the party is already dealing with separate investigations into other donations that Mr. Farage and Reform members accepted. The developments about the party’s finances have dragged down Reform’s popularity and threatened to undermine Mr. Farage’s leadership just as he tries to set the party on a path to government.

Mr. Farage is under parliamentary investigation over an undisclosed gift of 5 million pounds, about $6.7 million, from a British crypto-billionaire based in Thailand, while a separate police inquiry was opened into two donations from the mother of George Cottrell. Mr. Cottrell is another of Mr. Farage’s close aides.

In a statement, Bridget Phillipson, chair of the governing Labour Party, said, “Farage and Reform must cooperate with the authorities to establish the truth and prove just how deep this scandal goes.”

Last year, party supporters were almost giddy as they celebrated the rise of Reform. Mr. Farage was riding Europe’s wave of anti-immigrant, anti-establishment populism. His party was ahead in most polls, while the country’s Labour prime minister, Keir Starmer, was deeply unpopular. Mr. Farage described Reform as a “turquoise tide headed ever closer towards winning.”

Now, the future for Mr. Farage and his movement appears far less certain.

Reform’s popularity has been on a slow-but-steady, yearlong decline, even as it did well in municipal and regional elections in May. The Labour Party has a new leader and prime minister, and has begun to rise again in the polls. A new far-right party, Restore Britain, set up by a Reform defector, is causing Mr. Farage headaches. Even the Conservatives, who fell to a brutal defeat in 2024, are showing signs of political life.

In a BBC interview on Thursday broadcast before Channel 4 revealed the secretly recorded footage, Mr. Farage addressed the earlier allegations, saying that he had “broken no rules, done nothing wrong.” He also accused “people who hold positions of power, influence and money” of conspiring to politically damage him and his party.

But the scrutiny caused Mr. Farage to abruptly resign his seat in Parliament and then reclaim it last month. And he might be forced to face voters again within months if the parliamentary inquiry finds that he broke the rules by not disclosing the £5 million gift. The headlines about Reform’s victories in the 1,500 local elections in May have given way to persistent stories about his donors and the way that Reform is financed.

Reform officials had hoped to use the three-day conference to present the party as ready to govern. Speeches and sessions were set to be held in front of banners that read, “The First 100 Days,” a reference to what Mr. Farage has said would be aggressive, fast-paced changes if he becomes prime minister.

On Thursday, several members of the Reform leadership held forth at what the party called its “Business Day,” focusing on how they would lower taxes, strip away regulations, cut the size of government, harness artificial intelligence and increase spending on the military.

Robert Jenrick, a former Conservative minister who is now Reform’s representative on finance, pledged on Thursday that he would reassure financial markets by cutting £80 billion, about $108 billion, from government spending if the party wins power at the next general election, which must be held by 2029.

Mr. Jenrick has said that he sent a letter to major banks in Britain and the United States inviting top officials to round-table discussions in London and New York. “As chancellor, I will adopt sensible fiscal plans that shrink government borrowing relative to Labour’s plans,” he wrote in the letter, a copy of which was obtained by The New York Times.

In a group discussion on Thursday, Richard Tice, a former Conservative donor turned Reform lawmaker who now serves as Reform’s deputy leader, urged business leaders to participate in a months long “consultation” on how to stimulate the housing market if the party won power.

“Now, we’re not quite in government yet,” Mr. Tice conceded to the audience. But, he added, “Given how much we’re influencing government, sometimes it feels it.”

item.description:
When the Australian geologist and engineer Arnold Dix was approached by the Nepal authorities to help find those who could be trapped in hydropower project tunnels after a major flood last week, he knew there were several pressing challenges.

First, rescuers needed to locate the projects and their entrances, because everything had been “removed” by the force of the flood, Mr. Dix said.

“It took us the better part of a day or two, just to figure out where the power stations used to be and also to develop a plan as to how might we save people if they survived,” he said.

Hundreds of workers have been missing in the tunnels since last Wednesday, when a glacial collapse sent tsunami-like waves of water mixed with rock and debris through two river valleys, killing more than 1,300 people and leaving more than 4,000 missing in Nepal and neighboring China.

Nepal has built a robust hydroelectric industry, harnessing the fast-flowing waters in the Himalayas to generate electricity. Those projects require both manual and engineering work to construct tunnel systems deep into the earth. Many hydropower projects have been constructed along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli Rivers, which bore the brunt of the flooding.

Mr. Dix and his team’s efforts were focused on the Trishuli 3A hydropower project.

Mr. Dix’s team relied on engineering drawings of the structures underground, satellite imagery and old charts to try and identify any potential “Goldilocks zones” — a term Mr. Dix used to describe a small subterranean area “where a human being could have survived.”

This information would guide rescuers on where to start looking. Most of their efforts have been focused in the project’s cable tunnel — which runs from the underground powerhouse to the transmission grid, he said.

Those immense efforts paid off on Friday.

Mr. Dix said rescuers heard the “faint sound of someone in Nepalese acknowledging” their calls.

A short time later, at least two workers were found alive. They have been flown to Kathmandu for treatment. One is in a critical condition.

One of the rescued, Sanjay Sah, is a mechanical foreman and the other, Kabir Maharjan, is a mechanical supervisor, according to a list seen by The New York Times. Both were employees of the Nepal Electricity Authority, according to the list.

Rescuers also heard other voices in the tunnel, the people said, kindling hope that more people could be saved. It was not clear how many were still alive.

“I was in tears, of course,” Mr. Dix said of the moment he found out the good news.

For both survivors, challenges remain, he said. “They don’t know what’s happened; they’ve been cut off from the world the whole time, they’ve been trapped in the dark for more than a week,” he said.

“They’re going to find out that thousands of people have died, including their friends and colleagues,” he added.

There will be no rest for Mr. Dix. Once he arrives in Kathmandu on Friday evening, he will put what he has learned from this rescue “into strategies about how we might go and help other power stations.”

He said the efforts of the rescue team were extraordinary, adding, “we’re performing miracles out there.”

item.title: Philippines’ Vice President Faces Arrest Over Assassination Threats
item.description:
A Philippine court on Friday ordered the arrest of the country’s vice president, Sara Duterte, over charges that she threatened to have President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., the first lady and a former speaker of the House of Representatives assassinated.

It was the latest turn in the acrimonious, yearslong feud between Ms. Duterte and Mr. Marcos, former allies who are scions of two Philippine political dynasties.

The charges stem from a late-night news conference Ms. Duterte gave nearly two years ago, when she was being investigated for corruption. In the speech, she said that she had made arrangements for Mr. Marcos, his wife, Liza; and Martin Romualdez, the president’s cousin and the speaker at the time, to be assassinated if she were killed.

It was not the first time Ms. Duterte had spoken of violence against Mr. Marcos — a few weeks earlier she had threatened to behead him. But it elicited a response from the president, who did not name the vice president but spoke of “criminal intent.”

Last month, the Philippine Department of Justice filed a criminal case against Ms. Duterte. On Friday, a regional court in Quezon City issued a warrant on three counts of making “grave threats.” The court set bail at 120,000 pesos, about $1,900, for each count, which Ms. Duterte posted on Saturday morning, her lawyer Paul Lim told reporters. Her booking procedures were briefly delayed after Ms. Duterte refused to enter the court without her supporters, saying that she feared for her life and wanted witnesses present.

Ms. Duterte has said her comments about Mr. Marcos and his family were “maliciously taken out of logical context.” Her allies have argued that she cannot be criminally prosecuted while she is in office.

“Regardless of the question on jurisdiction, she has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies,” Mr. Lim said in a statement on Friday.

Around five years ago, Mr. Marcos and Ms. Duterte formed an unlikely alliance that propelled them to the two highest positions in the country. But their partnership collapsed quickly after the election, with both camps hurling accusations of corruption against the other.

The acrimony spiraled further last year, when Mr. Marcos facilitated the arrest of his predecessor, Rodrigo Duterte, who is Ms. Duterte’s father. He is facing charges at the International Criminal Court of crimes against humanity over his brutal antidrug campaign.

Ms. Duterte has faced other legal issues. She has been impeached twice and is currently facing trial in the Philippine Senate. A conviction would bar her from holding public office. But she remains the leading contender for president in the next election, which is scheduled for 2028.

item.title: Israel Says It Is Cementing Its Foothold in Southern Lebanon
item.description:
The Israeli defense minister said Friday that the military’s capture of a strategic ridge in Lebanon a day earlier had consolidated its foothold in the south of the country, adding to concerns that Israel intends to prolong its monthslong occupation there.

The Ali al-Taher ridge, about six miles from Lebanon’s border with Israel, sits above a sprawling underground base for Hezbollah, the Lebanese militant group that Israel has long fought.

The ridge had increasingly become a focal point of the conflict, which reignited in March after the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran, Hezbollah’s chief backer.

The Israeli defense minister, Israel Katz, said in a video statement that the capture of Ali al-Taher marked “the completion of the process of consolidating our hold on the security zone in southern Lebanon,” referring to an Israeli-occupied strip of Lebanese territory along the border.

Hezbollah’s media office did not respond to a request for comment on Israel’s claim that it had captured the ridgeline. The office of the Lebanese presidency declined to comment.

In June, Israel and Lebanon agreed to a U.S.-brokered framework intended to end the fighting and eventually restore Lebanese control over the country’s south. But the truce has frayed. Fighting between the sides has continued in southern Lebanon, including on Friday, when the Israeli military said it had begun a fresh round of strikes there in response to a Hezbollah drone attack on soldiers.

Under the framework, the Lebanese military would disarm Hezbollah and deploy in designated “pilot zones” in southern Lebanon as Israeli troops progressively withdrew. That process has largely stalled, however, with Israel and Hezbollah at odds over which side must act first. Hezbollah has consistently rejected demands to put down its weapons.

Orna Mizrahi, a former Israeli deputy national security adviser who specializes in Lebanon at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv, said that, in Israel’s view, the pilot zone experiment had failed because Lebanon was not doing enough to prevent Hezbollah from returning to areas vacated by Israeli troops. “The big question is what’s next,” she said.

Lebanese officials, for their part, have said that continued Israeli attacks and the lack of further military withdrawals have impeded the plan.

For months, Israel has said that its forces would remain in Lebanon until Hezbollah has been disarmed. Mr. Katz reiterated that in his statement on Friday, as the capture of the ridge underscored how entrenched the Israeli military has become in Lebanon, with little sign of an end to the occupation.

It remained unclear what Israel’s capture of the Ali al-Taher ridge would mean for the broader U.S. conflict with Iran. Tehran has insisted that any agreement to end that conflict must stop fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon.

Iran warned the United States on Thursday that Israel’s capture of the ridge would cross a red line and that Tehran would retaliate forcefully if the offensive continued, according to an Iranian official and a member of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps. The officials, who asked not to be named because they were discussing sensitive issues, said the message was sent via Oman.

The Revolutionary Guards official said that roughly 70 to 100 Hezbollah members, along with Iranian military advisers, had been trapped inside the complex beneath the ridge as Israeli forces encircled it.

The Israeli military said on Thursday that it had established “operational control” over the ridge after an operation that began in June, when thousands of Israeli troops surrounded the underground facility, one of Hezbollah’s largest in Lebanon, and trapped dozens of militants inside.

The Israeli military said its soldiers had cleared Hezbollah militants from two underground routes beneath the ridge, killing some while others fled. Mr. Katz said on Friday that the military would now work to neutralize the tunnels and deploy around the ridge to maintain its hold and prevent Hezbollah from re-establishing itself there.

Sarit Zehavi, the president of the Alma Research and Education Center, an Israeli group focused on security along the northern border, said the capture of the ridgeline was significant but would not fundamentally alter the state of the conflict.

“I don’t feel that it’s a different day,” she said. “There is still a lot of work to do.”

item.title: Russian Drone Strikes Office of Ukraine’s Intelligence Chief
item.description:
Russia attacked the headquarters of Ukraine’s domestic intelligence service in the heart of the capital, Kyiv, on Friday afternoon, aiming an exploding drone directly at the office of the agency’s director, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

The blast at the central building of the Security Service of Ukraine, across the street from the landmark St. Sophia Cathedral, came amid another day of intense bombardment in Kyiv as Russia and Ukraine are locked in an escalating air war.

Mr. Zelensky said on social media that the agency’s director, Oleksandr Poklad, had survived the strike. The Ukrainian leader added that he had ordered Mr. Poklad to devise a response that would mirror the Russian attack.

The strike in central Kyiv, which would be the equivalent of targeting a top Russian official in Red Square, was the latest sign that the red lines that still remain in Europe’s deadliest war in a generation continue to be crossed.

Emergency crews were responding at the scene of the attack. At least 12 people were injured, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.

The strike came as the American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were planning imminent visits to Moscow and to Kyiv to try to restart stalled negotiations aimed at ending the war, Ukrainian officials said.

Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said on social media that the Russian attack was “a major escalation” that demanded a response. “Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace — laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy,” he said.

Kyiv has been subjected to barrages of missiles and drones for more than a week. At least six people have died in strikes in the city in the past 24 hours.

On Thursday, a Russian strike destroyed a Coca-Cola bottling plant in the Kyiv region and a warehouse for the World Health Organization that stored humanitarian medical supplies.

Over the course of the war, the Security Service of Ukraine, known as the S.B.U., has been transformed from a conventional domestic counterintelligence service into a specialized deep-strike and sabotage force. It has executed some of the war’s most brazen operations inside Russia.

In 2022, the agency orchestrated a damaging truck-bombing on the Kerch Bridge, which connects Russia to occupied Crimea. Multiple road spans collapsed, and fuel tankers ignited on an adjacent railway.

S.B.U. operators attacked the bridge again in 2023, using maritime drones to target the structure’s support pillars.

Perhaps the most audacious assault came in 2025, when the agency smuggled into Russia dozens of strike drones and launchers inside truck containers disguised as cargo and prefabricated sheds. Ukraine used the drones to attack strategic air bases across Russia.

The S.B.U. headquarters is in one of the most secure parts of Kyiv. The street in front of the building has been closed to pedestrian traffic since the early months of the war. The building is near historical landmarks, busy cafes and apartment buildings.

St. Sophia’s Cathedral was not damaged, Ukrainian officials said, but some windows in other buildings on the grounds were blown out.

Stanislav Zavertailo, the owner of a nearby cafe, said that his business was destroyed.

“I don’t know what else to say,” he wrote on social media. “I’m heading there. I’m most worried about the guests and the team.”

One customer was taken to hospital, he wrote.

“It looks like the effects of the blast wave, with no bleeding or visible injuries,” he said. “The entire team is safe and unharmed, but they are still in shock.”

Following the attack, the S.B.U. vowed revenge.

“The Russians will receive a painful response to their strikes — more special operations, uncovered agent networks and eliminated enemies,” the agency said in a statement.

item.title: Behind the Investigations Into the Venezuelan Oilman Partnering With Trump
item.description:
Prosecutors in Spain targeted the Venezuelan oilman Alejandro Betancourt in one money laundering inquiry. Swiss authorities investigated him in another. Both countries requested his extradition from Britain, where Mr. Betancourt lives in a 14-bedroom country estate, and British authorities arrested him less than a year ago, barring him from traveling abroad.

All of it hardly mattered.

As part of the Trump administration’s takeover of Venezuela’s oil industry, the United States is forming an extraordinary partnership with Mr. Betancourt. Under the arrangement, the Pentagon could seek to take a large stake in his company, a deal that defies easy comparison in recent American history, oil analysts say.

That would make Mr. Betancourt the main partner of the Trump administration as it pushes not just to control the sale of Venezuela’s oil, but to own a chunk of it directly. And it would place Mr. Betancourt at the core of Venezuela’s deepening transformation from a sovereign nation into essentially a vassal state of the United States.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio brought up Mr. Betancourt in a White House meeting in the spring. He had decided that Mr. Betancourt could be a viable partner for the United States because he had experience forging oil deals in Venezuela and increasing production there, said a person familiar with U.S. efforts to support Mr. Betancourt.

That meant Mr. Betancourt would need to be able to travel freely. Officials from the State Department and the Justice Department intervened in the Swiss investigation by reaching out to Swiss counterparts to persuade them not to go forward with the extradition, according to people familiar with the matter.

They also asked Britain’s government to ease travel restrictions on Mr. Betancourt, the people said, allowing him to travel to Venezuela and to the United States to meet with Trump administration officials. The British government was reluctant but eventually agreed to the request.

Under the deal with the Trump administration, a financing office within the Pentagon plans to partner with Mr. Betancourt’s oil company, North American Blue Energy Partners, or NABEP, which is being granted 100-year concessions to operate 17 oil fields in Venezuela.

Mr. Betancourt does not own the fields, but the concessions give him the exclusive rights to exploit them — and they are potentially enormous. In all, these oil fields have estimated reserves of 65 billion barrels, nearly as much as all the proven reserves in the United States.

“The United States has wreaked havoc on us” with this deal, said Rafael Ramírez, a former Venezuelan energy minister. He called the unusual arrangement with Mr. Betancourt “grotesque” and “unsustainable in the long run” because it was done in secret with an authoritarian government many Venezuelans view as illegitimate, echoing criticism across Venezuela’s normally polarized political spectrum.

Sara Chouraqui, a spokeswoman for Mr. Betancourt and the general counsel for his oil company, rejected the criticism.

“To Alejandro, this isn’t political,” Ms. Chouraqui said. “The fact that he is now in a position to revitalize the country’s long-dormant economic potential is in itself a win, not for any one political party, but for all of Venezuela.”

This article is based on interviews with oil executives, current and former U.S. officials, and former Venezuelan officials, some of whom spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomacy.

In settling on Mr. Betancourt, the Trump administration opted against partnering directly with a U.S. oil giant like Chevron, which has had extensive operations in Venezuela for decades, or Petroleos de Venezuela, the country’s state-owned oil company.

The deal with Mr. Betancourt holds some parallels with the transition from state socialism to market capitalism in post-Soviet Russia, when the West worked with newly anointed oligarchs to gain access to Russian oil reserves.

“It’s actually eerily similar,” said Francisco Rodríguez, a Venezuelan economist. In both cases, Mr. Rodríguez said, weak governments handed over key parts of their oil industries to well-connected figures. In Russia, he noted, these oligarchs grew immensely rich while often supporting authoritarian rule.

In response to a request for comment on U.S. efforts to press Switzerland and Britain to lower the legal pressure on Mr. Betancourt, the State Department cited a briefing on Tuesday in which a top U.S. official told reporters that the administration had found “no pending legal problems in the United States.” The ongoing legal cases had largely originated from U.S. prosecutors’ efforts to look into Mr. Betancourt’s dealings about a decade ago, the official said.

The White House had no comment, while the Justice Department and the British Embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment. The Washington Post reported earlier on some details of U.S. efforts to help Mr. Betancourt with his legal challenges.

Explaining the deal, Mr. Rubio told a Venezuelan journalist this week that the partnership with Mr. Betancourt was “going to be professionalized” and will “operate under laws that will apply to it so that the money is never used improperly.”

President Trump has promoted the deal as a way to lower gasoline prices and replenish U.S. strategic oil reserves, though the effort could take years, at best, and there are questions about whether the Pentagon has the legal authority to pursue the deal.

Mr. Betancourt has a long history operating in the shadowy world of secretive oil deals, regime power struggles and multiple financial crime investigations.

But until news of the deal emerged in recent days, Mr. Betancourt, 46, born into an upper-crust family that traces its lineage to a 19th-century Venezuelan president, was largely known for mastering the art of landing deals with Venezuela’s authoritarian leaders while still in his 20s.

Reaping a bonanza from no-bid contracts with Venezuela’s government, he plowed that money into trophy real estate around the world, including a penthouse in Manhattan’s Olympic Tower and a castle in Spain with extensive hunting grounds, as he shifted into new ventures, from African banks to pumping Venezuelan oil.

While the deal with the Trump administration is unorthodox, there is strong reasoning for this new approach, according to Venezuelan oil experts.

Franco Sampieri, the director of the Petroleum Chamber of Zulia, the oil-producing state in western Venezuela, said he believed the deal would bring many direct and indirect jobs to the region.

“We are 30 years behind,” Mr. Sampieri said, emphasizing that Zulia desperately needed such an initiative to help resuscitate the industry.

Petróleos de Venezuela is a hollowed-out shell of what it once was, hobbled by mismanagement and corruption, dimming its allure as a potential partner. Mr. Betancourt also has a reputation, however marred by allegations of impropriety it may be, of getting business done and raising oil production in Venezuela.

The Trump administration may also have a kind of leverage over Mr. Betancourt that it couldn’t exert over a major U.S. oil company, especially after his arrest in Britain last November in connection to international money laundering inquiries.

If Mr. Betancourt doesn’t toe the line, the Trump administration could reverse course and press foreign legal authorities to revisit allegations, or push the Justice Department to reactivate its investigation into a U.S. money laundering case in Miami. In that case, Mr. Betancourt was identified, albeit not by name, as an unindicted co-conspirator, according to a person familiar with the case.

The help Mr. Betancourt has gotten from the U.S. government to evade further scrutiny — instead of its treating him as a potential witness in other corruption inquiries, or even as an unindicted co-conspirator — has shocked former Justice Department officials, the person familiar with the Miami investigation said.

Mr. Betancourt has recently become close to Mauricio Claver-Carone, a powerful political operator close to Mr. Rubio, according to two people with knowledge of their relationship. Mr. Claver-Carone has been instrumental in shaping Venezuela policy despite holding no formal role in the Trump administration.

Mr. Betancourt comes from a privileged background. His father was a cardiologist and pianist, and his mother a jewelry designer. He attended an elite private high school in Caracas before studying business at Boston’s Suffolk University.

When he returned to Venezuela, high oil prices were setting off an economic boom. Hugo Chávez’s revolution was in full swing as the Venezuelan leader sought to use oil revenues to consolidate power, fund antipoverty projects and lift Venezuela’s profile on the world stage.

But amid Mr. Chávez’s expropriations and anti-American rhetoric, there were also opportunities to make a great deal of money in a short amount of time. Mr. Betancourt cut his teeth selling turbines, which allowed him to develop ties with government officials.

Leveraging those contacts, Mr. Betancourt got into the business of building power plants at a time when Venezuela was experiencing electricity shortages. Despite having little experience in the power generation sector, Mr. Chávez’s government awarded him an array of no-bid contracts.

José Aguilar, an independent Venezuelan energy auditor who often coordinated his work with Venezuelan civic transparency organizations, found that Mr. Betancourt’s company overbilled state entities by more than $800 million for the power plants, often by tacking on massive markup fees.

Separately, prosecutors in Europe and the United States investigated claims that executives at Mr. Betancourt’s company paid tens of millions of dollars in bribes to secure the contracts.

Mr. Betancourt was not charged as a result of the multiple investigations into these activities, and Ms. Chouraqui, his spokeswoman, said he had never been charged with a crime in any jurisdiction.

Even so, Mr. Aguilar called the U.S. government’s decision to partner with Mr. Betancourt “shameful.”

All of Mr. Betancourt’s early deals laid the foundation for a rapid accumulation of wealth. But they also exposed him to scorn from many Venezuelans who viewed him as a traitor for dealing with a government that was jailing dissidents, purging the civil service of critics and nationalizing parts of the economy.

Mr. Betancourt made his foray into Venezuela’s oil industry in 2011 by acquiring a minority stake in Petrozamora, a state-controlled producer operating oil fields in Lake Maracaibo.

Coordinating with other minority owners from Russia, Mr. Betancourt held on to his stake in Petrozamora until 2022, when one of the Venezuelan government’s periodic purges pushed him out of the company at the behest of Tareck El Aissami, the oil minister at the time and a rival of Delcy Rodríguez, then the vice president.

But Mr. Al Aissami’s purge was short lived, and served as the catalyst for his own arrest in 2024 on corruption charges.

After his stake in Petrozamora was expropriated, Mr. Betancourt navigated the fallout by aligning with the regime faction led by Ms. Rodríguez, who is now Venezuela’s president, and her brother, Jorge Rodríguez, the head of the National Assembly.

He regained his stake in Petrozamora in 2024 through NABEP, a newly created company registered in Barbados. The company helped execute a rapid operational turnaround, lifting production from 20,000 barrels a day to about 200,000.

In doing so, NABEP emerged as the second-largest private oil company in Venezuela, coming within reach of Chevron’s production of about 280,000 barrels a day.

As the Trump administration tries to ramp up Venezuela’s overall oil output, that positioned Mr. Betancourt not only as a key interlocutor between Washington and Caracas, but someone poised to amass even greater wealth and power as a partner of the U.S. government.

Isayen Herrera contributed reporting.
